title: GANs in brief
summary: A GAN trains a generator G (noise → sample) against a discriminator D (sample → probability it is real). They play a minimax game over V(D, G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]. For a fixed G the best discriminator is p_data / (p_data + p_g), and against it G minimises the Jensen-Shannon divergence, so the game is won when the distributions match. In practice G uses the non-saturating loss −log D(G(z)); training can oscillate and collapse onto a few modes.
llm_link: LLMs are not GANs, but the adversarial idea appears around them: the autoencoders behind latent diffusion are sharpened with an adversarial loss, and learned 'discriminators' (reward models, classifiers that detect generated text) judge model outputs much as D judges G.
key_ideas: Goodfellow et al. (2014): generator G(z) maps noise to samples; discriminator D(x) ∈ (0, 1) is the probability x is real.
Value: V(D, G) = E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1 − D(G(z)))]; D maximises it, G minimises it.
Optimal discriminator: D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)). Then V(D*, G) = −log 4 + 2·JS(p_data ‖ p_g), minimised when p_g = p_data (D* = ½ everywhere).
Non-saturating generator loss: maximise log D(G(z)) instead of minimising log(1 − D(G(z))); it gives strong gradients when D confidently rejects fakes.
Failure modes: oscillation and mode collapse (few distinct outputs).
GANs sample in one pass (fast) but have no likelihood; diffusion trains with a stable regression objective and has overtaken GANs for many image tasks.

quiz.q: Predict the result: at a point x, p_data(x) = 0.3 and p_g(x) = 0.1. What does the optimal discriminator output there?
quiz.explain: D*(x) = 0.3 / (0.3 + 0.1) = 0.75: three times as likely to be real as fake at that point.

quiz.q: When the generator matches the data distribution exactly, what does the optimal discriminator output?
quiz.explain: p / (p + p) = ½: real and fake are indistinguishable, so the best D can do is a coin flip.

quiz.q: Why is the generator usually trained to maximise log D(G(z)) rather than minimise log(1 − D(G(z)))?
options: Early on, when D(G(z)) ≈ 0, log(1 − D) is flat and gives tiny gradients; −log D(G(z)) gives strong ones
It removes the need for a discriminator
quiz.explain: Both push D(G(z)) upward, but the non-saturating version has its steepest slope exactly where the generator is doing badly.

quiz.q: A GAN trained on faces keeps producing the same few faces. What is this called?
quiz.explain: The generator found a few outputs that fool D and stopped covering the variety of the data.

quiz.q: Which statement best compares GANs with diffusion models?
options: GANs sample in a single pass but train less stably; diffusion is slower to sample but trains with a regression loss
quiz.explain: Speed versus stability and coverage: one reason diffusion overtook GANs for many image tasks.

problems.title: Discriminator and generator losses (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
You are given the discriminator's outputs on a batch of real samples, d_real, and on a batch of generated samples, d_fake (arrays of probabilities). Write:

  • d_loss(d_real, d_fake) = −mean(log d_real) − mean(log(1 − d_fake)) (minimising this maximises V for D)
  • g_loss(d_fake) = −mean(log d_fake) (the non-saturating generator loss)
d_loss(np.array([0.5]), np.array([0.5]))   # 2·log 2 = 1.386
g_loss(np.array([0.5]))                     # log 2 = 0.693

tests.name: coin-flip discriminator
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = d_loss(np.array([0.5, 0.5]), np.array([0.5, 0.5]))
assert out is not None, 'd_loss returned None'
assert abs(out - 2 * np.log(2)) < 1e-9, f'a discriminator that always says 0.5 has loss 2 log 2 = 1.386, got {out}'

tests.name: good discriminator, low loss
tests.code:
import numpy as np
assert d_loss(np.array([0.99]), np.array([0.01])) < d_loss(np.array([0.6]), np.array([0.4])), 'confidently right answers should give a lower discriminator loss'

tests.name: fake term uses 1 - d_fake
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = d_loss(np.array([1.0]), np.array([0.2]))
assert abs(out - (-np.log(0.8))) < 1e-9, f'with d_real = 1 only the fake term counts: -log(1 - 0.2) = {-np.log(0.8):.4f}; got {out}'

tests.name: generator loss
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = g_loss(np.array([0.5, 0.5]))
assert out is not None and abs(out - np.log(2)) < 1e-9, f'expected log 2 = 0.693, got {out}'
assert g_loss(np.array([0.9])) < g_loss(np.array([0.1])), 'the generator loss should fall as D is fooled more'

problems.title: Why the generator loss was changed
problems.prompt:
Let d = D(G(z)). Compare how steeply each generator loss changes with d when the discriminator is winning (d close to 0). Write slopes(d) returning (minimax_slope, nonsat_slope), the derivatives with respect to d of

  • the original loss log(1 − d): derivative −1 / (1 − d)
  • the non-saturating loss −log d: derivative −1 / d

Then check the story: at d = 0.01 the non-saturating slope is about 100 times larger.

tests.name: values at d = 0.5
tests.code:
out = slopes(0.5)
assert out is not None, 'slopes returned None'
m, n = out
assert abs(m + 2) < 1e-9 and abs(n + 2) < 1e-9, f'at d = 0.5 both slopes are -2, got {out}'

tests.name: non-saturating is much steeper early
tests.code:
m, n = slopes(0.01)
assert abs(n / m) > 90, f'at d = 0.01 the non-saturating slope should be about 99x the minimax one, got ratio {n/m:.1f}'

tests.name: both push d upward

problems.title: The optimal discriminator (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
On a tiny world of 4 possible samples, p is the data distribution and q the generator's. Write best_d(p, q) = p / (p + q) (element-wise) and value(p, q, D) = Σ p·log D + Σ q·log(1 − D), the GAN value as sums over the 4 samples.

The tests check the two theorems from the video: when q = p, D* is ½ everywhere and the value is −log 4; otherwise the value at D* equals −log 4 + 2·JS(p, q), which is larger.

tests.name: matching distributions
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])
D = best_d(p, p)
assert D is not None and np.allclose(D, 0.5), f'when the generator matches the data, D* = 0.5 everywhere, got {D}'
v = value(p, p, D)
assert abs(v + np.log(4)) < 1e-9, f'the value at the optimum should be -log 4 = {-np.log(4):.4f}, got {v}'

tests.name: D* is p / (p + q)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
D = best_d(np.array([0.3, 0.7]), np.array([0.1, 0.9]))
assert np.allclose(D, [0.75, 0.4375]), f'expected [0.75, 0.4375], got {D}'

tests.name: value at D* = -log 4 + 2 JS
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([0.4, 0.4, 0.1, 0.1]); q = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]); m = (p + q) / 2
js = 0.5 * np.sum(p * np.log(p / m)) + 0.5 * np.sum(q * np.log(q / m))
v = value(p, q, best_d(p, q))
assert abs(v - (-np.log(4) + 2 * js)) < 1e-9, f'expected {-np.log(4) + 2*js:.5f}, got {v}'

tests.name: D* beats other discriminators
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([0.4, 0.4, 0.1, 0.1]); q = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])
best = value(p, q, best_d(p, q))
for D in (np.full(4, 0.5), np.array([0.9, 0.6, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([0.7, 0.7, 0.3, 0.3])):
    assert value(p, q, D) <= best + 1e-12, 'no discriminator should score a higher value than D*'

hints: value: np.sum(p * np.log(D)) + np.sum(q * np.log(1 - D))
